Weaponry (Experimental)

A fast multiplayer arena shooter, in 1v1, 2v2, and 3v3, where how you move matters as much as how you aim.

Design goal

Make movement the skill ceiling. Players can bunny hop, jump continuously, sprint, dash, and slide, and the maps are built with jumpable obstacles so good routes reward good movement. Two players with the same weapon should still look very different in a fight.

What I designed

  • Movement kit. Bunny hopping, continuous jumping, sprinting, dashing, and sliding.
  • Abilities with visible cooldowns. Slide and dash each have a clearly labeled icon, so players can see exactly when the cooldown ends and plan their next move.
  • Maps built for movement. Jumpable obstacles create different routes through each map.
  • Random weapon and map every round. A slot-machine-style screen reveals the next round, so players can't lean on a single loadout and have to adapt.
  • Match structure. First to 5 rounds, with a 60-second cap per round and overtime, so matches stay fast and nobody can stall.

What I changed

  • Slide was too strong. It was overpowered, so I cut its duration from 1.25 seconds to 1 second.
  • Rounds dragged. I capped each round at one minute to prevent long rounds.
  • Hit detection tradeoff. I first tried server-side hit validation with rollback, but the delay between network calls made valid hits fail. As a solo developer I moved to client-side hit detection, choosing responsiveness and stability over cheat resistance.

Where it started

Before the full game I built a playable prototype with sliding, running, wallrunning, a pick-up-and-throw weapon system, and a knife with custom melee animations. You can play it in your browser from the links on this page.

RoboLeague

A fast online 3v3 soccer game built around raw mechanics: dribbling, shooting, and defending. Released on Steam and Google Play.

Design goal

Make mechanical skill pay off. I wanted shots that take practice to learn and feel great to land, in a game that stays responsive enough for fast online play.

What I designed

  • Mouse-driven spin. Mouse movement sets the direction and strength of spin, which controls how much curve and height a shot gets. I applied spin to the ball directly because a Magnus force on the rigidbody alone wasn't enough.
  • Responsive third-person movement. A blend tree mixes walking, running, and strafing animations from the player's velocity, so movement reads clearly.
  • Abilities that change the match. Abilities like Powershot, Speedster, Trap, and Roulette dynamically influence the state of the pitch and the game, which keeps each match exciting and rewards players who master them.
  • Positions, including goalkeeper. Players join a team in a position such as forward, midfielder, or goalkeeper, and goalkeepers dive to save shots.
  • Practice mode, goalkeeper AI, and a tutorial. Players can spawn balls, place dummies, and turn on AI goalkeepers to learn the mechanics.
  • A mobile port with its own touch controls and UI.

What I changed

  • Ball synchronization, three attempts. A client-authoritative model felt instant but left players seeing different balls. A server-authoritative model with prediction and rollback kept fighting Unity's non-deterministic physics. I settled on a pure server-authoritative model.
  • The tradeoff. Everyone now sees the same ball, but responsiveness depends on each player's latency (about 90 to 300 ms on peer-to-peer). I chose consistency over instant feel and wrote up why.
  • Mobile controls. I ran a closed playtest group of 30+ community members to iterate on touch controls and UI/UX.
  • Performance. Profiling led me to remove redundant cameras, bake static lighting, and disable UI raycast targets, raising FPS by 150%.

Reaching players

I promoted the game through short-form video on YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok and ran a Discord community for feedback.

Results

How the ball sync evolved

Three designs for keeping one ball identical on every screen. The first two chased perfect responsiveness and ran into Unity's non-deterministic physics. The third accepts some latency in return for a ball everyone agrees on.

Top Bins: Free Kick Soccer

A 1v1 free kick game where the shot itself is the skill.

Design goal

Take what I learned from RoboLeague's spin system and build a whole game around it: every free kick should come down to how well you control curve, dip, and top-spin.

What I'm designing

  • Shot feel. I tuned top-spin, dip, and curl parameters so the ball responds predictably and rewards practice.
  • Goal feedback. Custom net cloth physics make scoring feel satisfying.
  • Game modes. A VS AI penalty shootout (5 kicks each) at Easy, Normal, or Hard; a practice mode with free kicks from anywhere; and online matchmaking or play-a-friend.
  • Real-time 1v1 online play. Matchmaking, synced turns, live chat, and network smoothing.
  • Cosmetics. A cosmetic-only shop with 40+ items across trails, balls, and stadiums in five rarity tiers, with textures, particle effects, and sounds generated in code.
  • Safe purchases. In-app purchases are checked server-side with Cloud Code, including a receipt verifier I wrote by hand, and rewards are rate-limited.

Status

Unreleased and in active development.

Built with

C#, Unity, Netcode, JavaScript cloud services, URP
